newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler plans 23,000 job cuts by 1999-paper.
newsitem.headline: Daimler plans 23,000 job cuts by 1999-paper.

text.p: A supervisory board member of the German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG said in a newspaper interview on Sunday that the group plans to reduce its workforce by 23,000 by 1999.

Walter Riester, deputy head of the German metalworkers union IG Metall and a member of Daimler-Benz's supervisory board, said the group planned to increase turnover by 26 percent by 1999, but that payroll would have to be cut by eight percent.

A spokesman for the group referred to comments by Daimler at its annual news conference earlier this month, when it said that the workforce would remain unchanged at around 290,000 for 1997. The spokesman made no other prognoses.
At the news conference, Daimler's head of personnel Heiner Tropitzsch said that the worst was over in terms of job losses at Germany's largest industrial group.
A report in an advance copy of Monday's Berliner Zeitung said that Daimler management's medium-term internal planning envisaged further job cuts, and Riester confirmed this in the report.
Riester said in the report that the job-cutting measures showed that the German government's plan to halve the numbers of unemployed in Germany by the end of the century were doomed to failure.
German unadjusted unemployment fell in March to 4.48 million from 4.67 million in February, which was the highest since 1933. The seasonally-adjusted figure fell by 15,000 to 4.30 million.

At the end of 1996, Daimler had around 290,000 employees, 21,000 less than the previous year. The job losses were mostly due to restructuring, which included the disposal of its AEG engineering and consumer products company and Dutch aircraft unit Fokker NV.
Daimler said that sales would "grow markedly" in the current year. The group reported sales of 106 billion marks for 1996 and an operating profit of 2.42 billion marks.
The previous year Daimler reported a record net loss of 5.7 billion marks.
